newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - MCI package gets strong response.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - MCI package gets strong response.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp said its MCI One consumer and small business telecommunication services package launched in April, has been its most popular offering ever, although not all services are yet available.

"It has been the most enthusiastically received product we have ever offered," Tim Price, chief operating officer of MCI's telecommunications business, told Reuters in an interview on Thursday. He declined to give detailed figures.
MCI One bundles local, long distance and international calling with Internet, cellular and paging all on one bill.
That is in theory. In practice, you can forget MCI local service if you are a consumer -- at least for now.

This is because MCI has to rely on its MCI Metro business network for local calling. It reaches 13 cities so far and is targeting 25 in early 1997. Even then it will not go much beyond central business districts to reach the suburbs.

MCI, like long distance rivals AT&T Corp and Sprint Corp, has not yet been able to reach any resale agreement with regional Bells to use their local service links to customers, as allowed under the 1996 Telecom Act.
"When we get local service it will go sky-high. Customers are saying 'come to us when you are ready,'" Price said.

A second snag is that MCI wireless unit Nationwide Cellular, despite its name, is not nationwide. By the end of the year it will reach 34 cities and 54 percent of the U.S. population, through the resale of the services of others.
By the middle of 1997, MCI's Personal Communications Services (PCS) resale deal signed last month with Nextwave Telecom Inc should provider broader coverage.

Price said that for MCI the importance of launching MCI One is that it has been able to get intelligent networks, customer service and especially billing systems ready -- and will add individual services as they become available.
On Thursday the company rolled out a bigger service bundle called networkMCI One including data, toll free and teleconferencing, all aimed at larger business customers.

Industry surveys suggest that customers want the simplicity of all their services from one provider with one bill, but of the big long distance companies only MCI so far has a billing system which will support it.

For MCI it should not only mean greater market share and more revenues -- at least until AT&T and Sprint catch up -- but a greater stability of customer base, which means lower administration and marketing costs.

In the meantime, MCI is embroiled in tough competition, particularly in the consumer market, where AT&T has been offering $100 checks to tempt across key customers. Loss of customers to rivals is called "churn" in industry speak.
"Residential churn is up this year because of (AT&T) checks, and I would say business churn is down," Price said.
He declined to give precise figures.
Price said AT&T's wholesale business, acting as a carrier of the communications traffic of companies that provide services but own no networks, was strong.
However he said wholesale's profit margins were too low for it to be a priority in investing new capital compared with meeting the needs of retail customers.
